title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In U.S. specialty pharma, list price is marketing; net realized price after 340B, PBM rebates, and Medicare Part D redesign is the only number that pays the dividend.
epigraph.author: Healthcare Payer & Channel Forensics

web_blocks.html: Gilead's distribution and gross-to-net (GTN) model splits into two distinct systems. One is high-volume pill and biologic shipping (HIV, Liver, Trodelvy, Veklury). The other is custom cell-therapy logistics (Kite). In the U.S., Gilead ships most small-molecule and biologic drugs through three big wholesalers (McKesson, Cencora, and Cardinal Health) and specialty pharmacies [1]. List prices for Biktarvy (~$4,200/month WAC) and Yeztugo (~$28,000/year WAC) face steep discounts before cash reaches Foster City. As a result, unit profits depend on Gilead's gross-to-net bridge. That bridge includes commercial PBM rebates, Medicaid rebates, 340B discounts, and the IRA Medicare Part D redesign [1].

Two channel forces shape Gilead's HIV profits from 2025 to 2028. First is 340B and government mix. U.S. HIV care relies heavily on Ryan White clinics and 340B hospitals, which receive statutory discounts of at least 23.1% plus inflation rebates. Second is the Medicare Part D redesign that began in January 2025. That law shifted catastrophic-phase costs onto drugmakers, requiring a 20% discount in that tier. Gilead reported a $1.1 billion hit to FY2025 HIV sales from Part D redesign. Even so, strong prescription volume lifted total HIV sales 6% to $20.8 billion [3, 4]. Next, CMS picked Biktarvy in January 2026 for IPAY 2028 Medicare price talks. The agency set a 38% Maximum Fair Price (MFP) cut to $2,600 per 30-day supply starting January 1, 2028. That cut creates an estimated $1.5 billion annual sales headwind that Yeztugo and cancer drugs must offset [15].

By contrast, Kite's cell-therapy supply chain is an engineering-heavy, patient-by-patient network. Kite runs GMP plants in El Segundo (California), Frederick (Maryland), and Hoofddorp (Netherlands), plus a viral-vector site in Oceanside. It keeps >96% batch success rates and 14–17 day vein-to-vein turnaround across hundreds of treatment centers. That reliable turnaround helps hospitals avoid long waitlists and failed patient batches. Small-molecule pills earn >88% gross margins. Custom CAR-T therapies earn lower margins (~65%–70% before amortization) due to single-batch labor, viral vectors, release testing, and cold-chain couriers. Across the whole company, small-molecule virology still drives the mix. That mix produced a 78.8% GAAP gross margin in FY2025 ($23,209 million gross profit on $29,443 million revenue) and over 86% non-GAAP product gross margin [1, 3].

web_blocks.takeaway: Gilead's blended cash-flow resilience stems from small-molecule virology economics (~88%+ gross margin, $563M CapEx on $29.4B revenue), even as IRA Part D redesign and 2028 MFP test HIV net pricing.

web_blocks.title: U.S. Manufacturing CapEx Cycle ($32B Through 2030)
paragraphs: FY2025 CapEx was a modest $563 million (1.9% of revenue). However, Gilead has outlined up to $32 billion in U.S. plant and R&D spending through 2030 [1]. This plan covers domestic biologics, ADC, and cell-therapy sites. Investors should watch if annual CapEx rises from ~$0.6B toward $1.0B–$1.5B/year, which would trim FCF conversion from ~111% of GAAP net income.

book_paragraphs: In U.S. biopharma, the list price printed on a pharmacy database is largely a fiction. What actually pays Gilead's R&D bills and its $4 billion annual dividend is the net realized price after three giant tollbooths take their cut: pharmacy benefit managers, the federal 340B hospital discount program, and Medicare Part D. If you want to understand why Gilead's HIV revenue grew 6% in 2025 despite strong prescription volume—and why management spent so much time on 2026 earnings calls talking about policy—you have to trace the gross-to-net bridge.

Start with 2025. When the Inflation Reduction Act's Medicare Part D redesign went live in January 2025, it eliminated the old coverage-gap donut hole and capped seniors' out-of-pocket drug spending. In exchange, drugmakers had to pick up 20% of the tab in the catastrophic phase. Because HIV patients stay on therapy year-round and routinely cross into the catastrophic tier, Gilead absorbed a $1.1 billion gross-to-net headwind in 2025 alone. Think about that: Biktarvy and its sister drugs had to grow underlying prescription volume by more than $2 billion just to deliver $1.2 billion of reported net HIV growth.

Then came the next shoe in January 2026: CMS selected Biktarvy for the third cycle of Medicare Drug Price Negotiation, setting a Maximum Fair Price of $2,600 for a 30-day supply—a 38% cut—effective January 1, 2028. Management estimates that cut will trim roughly $1.5 billion from annual Biktarvy sales starting in 2028. That is why Yeztugo's rapid launch in HIV prevention and Trodelvy's first-line breast cancer expansion are not nice-to-haves; they are essential earnings bridges across 2028.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Look at the FY2025 cash waterfall: $29.44 billion of revenue turns into $23.21 billion of gross profit, $10.02 billion of GAAP operating income, and $9.46 billion of free cash flow after just $563 million of CapEx. Very few businesses on earth convert nearly one-third of every revenue dollar into free cash flow—which is why Gilead can absorb a $1.1 billion Part D hit without breaking stride.

book_subsections.title: Inside the FY2025 Cash Waterfall
paragraphs: Walk down the FY2025 income statement with me line by line, because it reveals how clean Gilead's underlying unit economics really are when M&A write-downs aren't distorting the picture. Total revenue was $29,443 million. Cost of goods sold was just $6,234 million—leaving a 78.8% GAAP gross margin (and over 86% on a non-GAAP product basis once you strip out Kite acquisition amortization).

From that $23,209 million gross profit, Gilead spent $5,799 million on core R&D, $5,774 million on SG&A, $1,024 million on acquired IPR&D, and roughly $590 million on a partial impairment of its MYR Hepatitis Delta asset. Even after all of that—and $2,780 million of embedded depreciation and amortization—GAAP operating income came in at $10,022 million, a 34.0% operating margin. After $1,024 million of interest expense, $798 million of net interest and investment income, and $1,286 million of taxes (a remarkably low ~13.1% effective tax rate), GAAP net income reached $8,510 million. Cash flow from operations hit $10,019 million, and CapEx was just $563 million, leaving $9,456 million of free cash flow.

book_subsections.title: Two Supply Chains Under One Roof
paragraphs: Operationally, Gilead runs two completely different factories. Its small-molecule HIV and liver pills are manufactured through standard chemical synthesis and distributed through the big three wholesalers—McKesson, Cencora, and Cardinal Health—with minimal working-capital friction. By contrast, Kite's cell-therapy plants in El Segundo, Frederick, and Hoofddorp operate like bespoke hospital laboratories, turning each patient's frozen T-cells into Yescarta or Tecartus in 14 to 17 days with a >96% manufacturing success rate.

That manufacturing reliability is a genuine competitive moat in CAR-T, where rival cell therapies have historically struggled with out-of-specification batches and multi-week waitlists. Yet bespoke batches are expensive, and as Kite's 2026 volumes dipped mid-teens, fixed cleanroom overhead weighed on segment margins. Getting anito-cel approved in December 2026 is critical not just for top-line growth, but to fill Kite's existing manufacturing suites with high-margin multiple myeloma volume.
